entities.name: Laodice
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Laodice, a Hellenistic princess of the Seleucid Empire, played a crucial role in the intricate dynastic and diplomatic landscape of the 3rd century BCE, solidifying alliances through marriage. Born to Antiochus II Theos and Laodice I, she was a younger sister to future Seleucid monarchs Seleucus II Callinicus and Antiochus Hierax. Her life, though less documented than her male relatives, exemplifies the strategic deployment of royal women to secure geopolitical stability and dynastic continuity in the post-Alexandrian world. Her marriage to Mithridates II of Pontus was a pivotal event that shaped the power dynamics in Asia Minor, connecting two significant Hellenistic kingdoms.

Her primary historical significance stems from her marriage to Mithridates II of Pontus, a union orchestrated around 250-245 BCE. This marriage, a cornerstone of Seleucid foreign policy, aimed to secure an alliance with the rising Kingdom of Pontus, particularly as the Seleucid Empire faced internal strife and external pressures from Ptolemaic Egypt during the Third Syrian War (246–241 BCE). As Queen of Pontus, Laodice bore Mithridates III, who would succeed his father, thus embedding Seleucid lineage within the Pontic royal house. This diplomatic maneuver was intended to stabilize the northern Anatolian frontier and potentially provide a bulwark against other regional powers, including the Galatians.

Laodice's marriage fostered a period of relative stability between the Seleucid realm and Pontus, contributing to the complex web of Hellenistic inter-state relations. It ensured a crucial, albeit temporary, alliance that allowed the Seleucids to focus on other fronts, while also legitimizing the Pontic kingdom through its connection to the venerable Seleucid dynasty. Her progeny, Mithridates III, continued the line, ensuring that the influence of this strategic union rippled through subsequent generations of Pontic rulers, many of whom would later challenge Roman hegemony in the East.
